To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

French Canadian patients are more likely to show social symptoms and to show somatic complaints, whereas British Canadians are more likely to be concerned with guilt feelings, thought disorder, and organicity.

British Canadians are more likely than French Canadians to be admitted to a mental hospital for an acute episode, but are less likely to be readmitted for a chronic illness, and that French Canadians are more likely to have a functional disorder, but are less responsive to psychotherapeutic treatment.
French Canadians and British Canadian mental patients differ in the symptomatology, course, and treatment outcome of their illness.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the differences between British and French Canadians in the incidence, symptomatology and treatment of mental illness.

differences in the incidence and symptomatology of mental disorder among French and British Canadians and with the implications of these differences for the treatment of patients of these two ethnic origins.
the differences in the symptomatology and treatment of the mental disorders of two ethnic groups in Canada.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the differences between the two groups are not great, and the differences that are found are probably due to differences in the social and cultural background rather than to any inherent differences in the two groups of people themselves.

the French Canadian is more concerned with his social relationships and with the support that goes along with them, and that the British Canadian is more concerned about his intra-psychically derived relationships, his guilt, and his thought disorders.

the British Canadian patient is more concerned with his own personal and interpersonal relationships, whereas the French Canadian patient is more preoccupied with the relationships of others to him, with the social and interpersonal context.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is no single mental disorder, but rather a series of mental disorders, and that these are distributed among various social and ethnic groups.
